title: The Influencer Industrial Complex is Warping Local Politics
content:
In late February, Alexis Rose Hinkley, a Los Angeles influencer with over 1.1 million followers on TikTok and more than half a million on Instagram, sent an email to Rae Huang’s campaign with a proposal. She touted her “large, highly engaged following” and asked the campaign for payment. She wanted $2,000 per month for a minimum of six months for “strategic messaging” and helping to “translate policy priorities into compelling, authentic content,” according to an email verified by the campaign.

“If the campaign can help build a platform and framework that allows me to put my audience behind Rae without compromising the trust I’ve established, this collaboration can expand,” she wrote. That expansion “would include a full public online endorsement and a coordinated push to galvanize other creators and influencers.”

Huang’s campaign balked. They had not yet hit the city’s matching program for fundraising and were subsisting entirely on small dollar donations. They certainly didn’t have the money to pay an influencer thousands of dollars per month. They made it clear to Hinkley that she would not be paid. Hinkley stopped responding and soon began consulting for Nithya Raman, whom she now uses her platform to support.

Subscribe now

Over the past decade, the media landscape has shifted tremendously, and that shift has been even more pronounced in Los Angeles. YouTube is now the largest streaming service, traditional Hollywood production companies are floundering, and the job market is collapsing as more young writers, producers, and actors seek to make a living on Instagram and TikTok. The political news landscape has evolved too. Voters are getting their news from content creators on TikTok, X, YouTube, and Instagram. 53% of U.S. adults get their news from social media, and 38% of people aged 18 to 29 regularly consume news from news influencers, according to a report by Pew Research Center. But influencers, particularly in the political space, are not bound by any ethical standards, nor do they usually disclose when they’re working with political campaigns.

This has been a problem plaguing the national political landscape for a while, but now influencers are meddling in more statewide and city races. Andrew Cuomo’s campaign did outreach to MAGA influencers in his runoff against Zohran Mamdani, who was supported by a coalition of local influencers across the city working under the collective Creators for Zohran. Jasmine Crockett paid a D.C.-based political influencer to work for her campaign and push out messaging in the Texas primary senate race against James Talarico. Most recently, the California governor’s race was upended by influencers who helped break the story of abuse accusations against Eric Swalwell.

When an account run by Hinkley called Creators For LA popped up in January with the goal of rallying progressive influencers in Los Angeles, many content creators began following the page and collaborating with it on coverage of things like the anti-ICE protest in L.A. and the Bernie Sanders rally for a billionaire tax held in DTLA.

In between their coverage, the Creators for LA account shared selfies and videos from different L.A. political influencers along with memes. Hinkley also started a Creators for LA group chat with dozens of L.A. political influencers.

Early on, Creators for LA began promoting certain political candidates. The group was promoting Marissa Roy for LA City Attorney and Eunisses Hernandez for City Council. On February 20th, Hinkley invited other influencers in the Creators for LA collective to a dinner at Nativo in Highland Park with Hernandez, where they could meet her and make content. The creators also organized to support Faizah Malik’s city council run.

At first, the Creators for LA account appeared to support of Huang for mayor. On February 18th, Creators for LA posted a video of Huang speaking to political influencer Josh Greene. The video was captioned, “Would you like to see a Mayor who actually represents working people? 👏” A top comment on the video reads, “THAT’S MY MAYOR 🔥🔥🔥.”

Share

Influencers in the Creators for LA group chat back then seemed to be aligned on supporting Huang. Huang had recently collaborated with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, and progressive influencers were coalescing around her.

But by late March, the Creators for LA page took a turn. The account began cropping up in the comment section of other viral posts about L.A. politics, casting doubt on Huang’s ability to win. The Creators for LA account also suddenly began officially collaborating with Nithya Raman’s Instagram page and promoting her campaign.

Discussion broke out in the influencer group chat on who to endorse. “As for mayor, it would be good to collaboratively decide on Rae or Nithya... I’m having trouble sorting that one out,” Michael Mezzatesta, a political influencer and podcaster with 282,000 Instagram followers posted. After information was shared about the primary election on June 2nd, one influencer asked the group, “Are we going Rae at the primary or wut?”

“We’re gonna have to pick the most progressive and ALL rally behind them so we don’t divide votes and beat Bass,” Josh Green said in the chat.

Share

But according to creators in the Creators for LA group chat, Hinkley did not initially disclose that she had begun consulting for Raman’s campaign behind the scenes, even gaining admin access to Raman’s official Instagram account and collaborating with a slew of influencers and pages including Creators for LA.

Raman’s campaign first said that Hinkley was brought on as a paid consultant, but later clarified that they had actually never issued payment to her. Hinkley said that “there was a conversation about me joining in a paid capacity in the general,” however her time with the campaign ended before that happened and she is no longer consulting for Raman. She accused Huang’s team of running a smear campaign. “The lies Rae’s team have spread about me were insane have caused extreme stress for me and my partner,” she said.

Despite the Creators for L.A. fallout, both Huang and Raman have done intense outreach to the L.A. content creator community. Huang has hosted round tables aimed at learning more about the needs of influencers in Los Angeles. Raman has been building out her digital team. Last week, Raman appeared on Hasan Piker’s stream. After a litany of tough questions, Piker seemed to endorse her saying that, “out of the three candidates with viability she’s obviously a million times better than Karen Bass and certainly Spencer Pratt.”

But the Creators for LA drama reveals the messy dynamics at play in these local races that are increasingly being shaped by influencer discourse. Decisions about who to rally behind are being shaped across Instagram pages and Signal groups, often among influencers who have not publicly disclosed their tight, sometimes monetized, relationships with different candidates.

Potential consulting gigs, sponsored content opportunities, or the ability to gain attention by being close with an up and coming candidate can all influence about who a political influencer decides to throw their massive platform behind and why.

Some content creators are seemingly motivated by money, joking in chats about charging for interviews. But the bigger motivation is often access and clout (which of course turn into money later on).

Many political influencers build their entire platforms off access to politicians. Having a nationally known lawmaker, up and coming candidate, or political figure in your content will draw eyeballs, and so it is crucial for them to remain in the good graces of people in power.

This creates a lot of perverse incentives. Influencers will try to hitch their platform to a winning ticket early, seeking to grow their followings off candidates who have organic hype. Generations of MAGA influencers have done this with Donald Trump. More recently, it’s been happening with Democrats.

For instance, as Zohran Mamdani gained a larger and larger following during his runoff against Cuomo, D.C.-based political influencers who previously denounced his leftist policies ceased criticizing him and began begging the campaign for access, in some cases even pretending to be from New York in order to attend events for NYC creators.

As one candidate’s staffer recently explained it, these politicians are using influencers to get views and attention, but the influencers are also using the candidates. This dynamic is drastically different from traditional journalists, who are assigned to report on specific races or beats and do not develop the same symbiotic relationships with the candidates they’re covering.

This problem will likely only get worse as Democrats try to develop tighter relationships with content creators ahead of 2026, and content creators increasingly seek to grow their proximity to people in political power for money and clout.

One creator joked to me recently that if Democrats won the midterms it would be “good for his brand.” He was joking but he was also right, it would be good for his brand. If certain Democrats that he has gained access to and collaborated with get more political power, that influencer will also be elevated and money and mainstream attention will follow. He will profit.

This dynamic does not result in power being held to account. Hasan Piker has done a great job of asking candidates hard questions and refusing to build a platform based on access. But that posture is not the norm. We already have plenty of access journalism in the legacy media, we don’t need more of it proliferating on social media.

The dynamics emerging around these local races like the LA mayoral election will soon be replicated in cities across the country during upcoming election cycles, and most voters will never have a clue what’s going on.

If political influencers want to be taken seriously as journalists, (as they constantly claim they do!) they need to start adhering to basic journalistic ethics guidelines around disclosure, and they need to be willing to bite the hands that feed them. We don’t need more influencers auditioning for consulting gigs and seeking proximity to power, we need more content creators willing to challenge it.
